en: Now begins the first chapter:
[I bow] to the beloved, the peaceful, whose nature is the joy of the hearts of all living beings, the supreme,
the self of all, the infinite, the primordial, the stainless, the sole refuge of the universe, and the absolute.

We ever worship that certain fair-complexioned Lord, whose supreme form is the singular essence of the nectar of devotion, who is beloved solely by the devotion of his devotees, and who assumes the state of being possessed by devotion. 1.
With a form bound by the moon of illusion and the fire of desire,
sporting through his own power as an ocean of the nectar of names,
his essential form is that which can be reached only through names.
He whose nature is name, who brings delight through names. ||2||
Because there is no difference between Bhakti and Īśa, Kṛṣṇacaitanya is spoken of [as one];
yet for those who know the ultimate reality, the distinction between Kṛṣṇa and Bhakti is well known. (3)
Janārdana, who possesses both name and form, is renowned as the Name-Cintāmaṇi;
he himself is Kṛṣṇacaitanya, and his mantra consists of his very name. (4)

In this matter, one should not even entertain thoughts of enemies or friends based on the divisions of the zodiacal signs; for the Lord of the World is the soul of all, the kinsman of all, and the friend of all. (5)
All are qualified for the rituals of worship, conduct, recitation, and so forth therein.
The Manus have many times bestowed upon him dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa; they bestow upon the virtuous bhakti toward the Bhagavat, and in some instances, they bestow love.
If this work, which illuminates devotion according to the rules like moonlight from the moon,
is called *Bhakticandrikā* (The Moonlight of Devotion) by the wise,
then for that purpose, the procedure for the practice of mantras is here described in due order. (8)
Therein, first one should extract the mantras, and then the rules for conduct in due order;
he who recites the mantra by that very [method] attains supreme accomplishment. (9)
I shall proclaim the extraction of the mantra for the sake of accomplishing all desires and aims:
Kāma, Dharitrī, Māyā, and Indu constitute Ratipriya. (10)

The letter *a* (aja), followed by the fire-syllable (*va*), joined with the half-moon (*amāyukta*), and further conjoined with the supreme (*para*)—this is the seed-mantra named *prema*, which bestows the devotion of love. ||11||
Kṛṣṇacaitanya is the supreme mantra, beginning with *ṅe* and ending with *vahijāya*; by the recitation of this very mantra, a person attains all perfections. 12.
One should join the seed-syllable *hrīṃ* and the lotus-seed (*kamalābīja*) with each [name] beginning with Rāma;
likewise, one should place Nṛsiṃha in the position of Kāma. This sixfold mantra, beginning with the Vedas, accomplishes everything by itself, especially loving devotion. ||13||
Whosoever should mutter even one of these mantras is a great sage;
he is praised by all the gods and is the most excellent of the Bhāgavatas. 14.
Now I shall explain the procedure for conduct (*caryāvidhi*), which accomplishes the purpose of all mantras;
for without it, a mantra does not become effective through recitation and other such practices. (15)
Having risen during the Brāhma-muhūrta, the practitioner of steady intellect should meditate upon the pure Guru, fair-complexioned and smiling-faced, within the lotus of his forehead. (16)
Wearing white garlands and garments, adorned with bright sandalwood paste, seated upon a svastika posture, with his lotus-like hands forming the gesture of exposition (vyākhyā-mudrā). ||17||
Having meditated thus, one should purify one's own body with the dust from his lotus feet,
and then, having contemplated the Lord of Gods within the heart, [one should place him] upon those lotus feet.

Having risen in the morning, one should recite the mantra according to one's capacity while contemplating oneself as being identical with that [deity]. Then, having gone to a body of water for the purpose of bathing, and having bathed, one should draw a square mandala in the water. (19)
In that very context, it is said: "Now, by which mantra the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) should visit the sacred fords (tīrthas):
O Gaṅgā, O Yamunā, O Godāvarī, O Sarasvatī... (20).
"O Narmadā, Sindhu, Kāverī, be present in these waters!"—with this very goad-mantra and mudrā, [one draws the water] from the solar orb. ||21||

There, having recited the mantra eight times, having placed his joined palms upon his head eight times, and having bathed there three times, the wise man should perform the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) and other rites.
Having uttered the name "Kṛṣṇacaitanya" preceded by the word "kāmaṃ prema," one should offer twenty-five handfuls of water with the mantra: "I satisfy [Him] with reverence. (23)
Having given gifts and performed the ritual bath according to the rules, the best of practitioners,
having become pure, should sit at the doorway of the worship chamber and,
after duly worshipping the door-keepers, cross the threshold. ||24||
Then—one should perform the rite for pacifying spirits even while seated;
those spirits who dwell here upon the earth or in the sky [should be appeased]. (25)
O Earth, by you the worlds are supported; O Goddess, you are supported by Viṣṇu.
Therefore, support me always and make this seat pure. (26)
Having thus addressed the seat with the mantra, and having worshipped it there with the five [offerings] beginning with *dhārā*, the best of practitioners, facing east, [should proceed]. (27)
Seated in the svastika posture, having struck the left foot three times and raised the hands three times above the head, one should cast the gaze outside the temple.
One should expel those obstacles that are terrestrial, atmospheric, and celestial. ||29||
Then—
the practitioner, having purified his two hands with the Astra-mantra, with scents, and with flowers,
should again sprinkle those scents, flowers, and water with the Astra-mantra. (30)
Having rendered [the vessel] immortal with the root mantra, one should perform the supreme consecration;
thereafter, one should perform the binding of the directions with a crystal. 31.
Having constructed a triple enclosure of fire, one should stand in its center and perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) in due order with undistracted mind.

The one of pure intellect [is composed] of the organs of knowledge and action, the five gross elements, the five subtle elements, primordial nature (prakṛti), the mind (manas), the intellect (buddhi), and the ego (ahaṃkāra). ||33||

Then, having led the individual soul (jīva) along the path of the *suṣumṇā* together with its respective functions and having united it with Brahman, one should effect the identification [with the thought]: "I am He. || 34 ||
Having contemplated the body as empty, the wise one of purified intellect should diligently recite the sixteen seed-syllables of wind through the left nostril. (35)
Having drawn in the air through the left nostril alone,
one should then cause the circle of wind (vāyu-maṇḍala) situated at the navel to expand by means of that breath.
Having thoroughly purified [the body] with that effort, one should again [visualize] the person— the mass of sins— situated in the left side of the belly, dark-complexioned and with blood-red eyes.
Measuring only one thumb's breadth, it is then turned downward;
having diligently restrained the breath, one should recite [the mantra] sixty-four times.
Reciting it thirty-two times, one should slowly release it through the right [nostril]. ||39||
Again, having drawn in the wind through the right [nostril] with the fire-mantra, the practitioner of mantra should indeed arrest it by means of the yoga of breath-retention (kumbhaka). 40.
Having kindled the fire with the wind and completely consumed the sinful body, one should expel that wind, together with its ashes, outwardly by means of the *vāmā* [nāḍī]. ||41||
Having drawn in the breath through the left [nostril] while reciting the seed-syllable known as "Moon," one should place it in the moon of the forehead from the middle of the navel.
Having restrained the wind by means of the Vāruṇa [mudrā] and having brought about a shower of nectar from that lunar orb, he rendered his body immortal by means of that [shower]. ||43||
Having contemplated and made the body firm once again with the seed-syllable of Śakti,
one should meditate upon it and expel the breath through the right nostril alone.
One should re-establish the previously placed vital principles (jīva) and others in their respective locations;
then, one should perform the placement of the vital principle (jīvanyāsa) with the mantra "Haṃsa. (45)
I shall now declare the Jīvan-yāsa mantra, the most excellent limb of all ritual acts: the beginning of the Vedas (Om) with a bindu, followed by Śeṣa (Sa), Śakti (Ha), and Aṅkuśa (Kṣa). 46.
Reciting again the previous mantra: "Cādi-lāntam sendukhaṇḍam," "Ho Haṃsaḥ So'ham eva ca," and "Mama prāṇā iha prāṇāḥ. (47)
Reciting the mantra again in this manner: "May my life-breath remain here;
likewise my speech, mind, skin, sight, and hearing thereafter. (48)
OṂ GHRĀṆAPRĀṆĀ IHĀGATYA SUKENEVA CIRAṂ PUNAḤ TIṢṬHANTU SVĀHĀ;
this is the fourfold preceding seed-syllables followed by the wife of fire (Svāhā). 49.
The mantra for the placement of the living soul (jīvanyāsa) has been proclaimed by the Tantrikas, the most excellent among those who know mantras. ||50||
Thus ends the first chapter of the Bhakticandrikā.
Now begins the second chapter:
Thereafter, the most excellent practitioner should perform the Mātṛkā-nyāsa.
The seer of this mantra is Brahmā, and Gāyatrī is said to be its meter. ||1||
The mother Sarasvatī is to be meditated upon; she is called the deity by the wise.
The consonants are the seeds according to the knowers of reality, and they are the powers (śaktis) according to the best among those who know mantras. (2)
Then, following the sequence, the vowels are employed in the Mātṛkā-nyāsa;
having performed the fivefold placement upon the head, face, heart, genitals, and feet. (3)

One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the hands and limbs using the six vowels in pairs—beginning with *brahmā* (a), *indu* (i), and so on—placed at the beginning and end [of each syllable]. Then, one should meditate upon Sarasvatī.
Her face, arms, waist, and chest are adorned with the fifty letters of the alphabet;
she wears a radiant crown bound with a crescent moon, possesses full and lofty breasts,
and holds in her lotus-like hands a mudrā, a rosary, a jar brimming with nectar, and a book.
I take refuge in the Goddess of Speech, who possesses three eyes and bears a brilliant luster. ||5||
Having meditated thus, the wise practitioner should place the letters of the Mātṛkā upon his body.
On the head, the circumference of the face, the two eyes, the two ears, and then on the pair of nostrils, the two cheeks, the region of the lips,
the pair of lower teeth, the forehead, and the mouth.
One should arrange the letters corresponding to the vowels, the Vasus, and the pairs [of Yugas], conjoined with Indra.
One should place the letters from *ka* to *na* at the joints of the hands and feet;

the *pa*-group (*pavarga*) conjoined with the moon (*śa*) on both sides; *ya* and *ra* on the back and the navel respectively; and *la* in the belly, while *ya* and *ra* are situated in the heart and the right shoulder.
And on the left shoulder, one should likewise [place] the syllable *laṃ*. ||8||
One should then place the letters from *śa* to *kṣa*, adorned with the moon (*i*), upon the two hands, the two feet, the belly, the face, and the heart and the regions preceding it.
In these aforementioned locations, one should place the vowels together with the *visarga* and the consonants;
furthermore, within these very places, one should also place them joined with the *bindu* and the *visarga*.
By thus placing the letters of the *mātṛkā*, one becomes the very embodiment of the letters. ||10||
Then the excellent practitioner should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of Śrī Vāsudeva and the others;
for this very king of placements, Nārada is indeed the sage (*ṛṣi*). (11)
The meter is Gāyatrī, Vāsudeva is the deity, the seed-syllable is the Praṇava (Om), and Svāhā is proclaimed as the power (Śakti). ||12||
O virtuous lady, the presiding deity should be the goddess Kātyāyanī;
one should perform the five-limbed ritual with the mantra "ācakrāya," and thereafter, one should meditate upon her. 13.
One should meditate upon Him whose splendor is like the glow of refined gold, who is most beautiful, clad in yellow garments, and serene;
whose chest is radiant with the Śrīvatsa mark and adorned with the shimmering Kaustubha gem and divine ornaments;
who holds a slightly opened lotus, a mace, and a discus in His lotus-like hands, and whose very form is bliss.
Vāsudeva, the supreme lord, the jewel among immortals, who is served by Lakṣmī and occupies the throne of heaven. ||14||
Having meditated thus, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the forms and powers of the letters of the Mātṛkā.
I shall now declare the extraction of the mantra according to the sequence of its ritual application.

The Praṇava, the letters of the Mātṛkā, the Mūrti-mantra, and the Śakti-mantra ending in the dative suffix Ṅe; the mantra joined with the wife of Vahni (Svāhā) is to be employed in the place of the individual letters. ||16||
Vāsudeva is remembered as being joined with Lakṣmī; Ananta is endowed with Śakti;
Hṛṣīkeśa is joined with Śrī; and likewise, Saṅkarṣaṇa is joined with Prīti.
Viṣṇu is united with Padmālayā; Vaikuṇṭha is with Ramā;
Mādhava is joined with Kamalā; and the lotus-eyed one is with Kānti. ||18||
Through all-pervasiveness he is Viśvanātha, and likewise through peace he is Viśveśvara;
through detachment he is Nārāyaṇa, and through being endowed with intellect he is Nara. ||19||
Keśava is conjoined with Kīrti; Devakīnandana is conjoined with Śruti;
Pareśa is conjoined with Parā; and Parameṣṭhin is conjoined with Śobhā.
These are declared to be the Śaktis and Mūrtis of the vowels, according to their sequential application.
Now I shall describe, with effort and in due order, the forms and powers of the consonants:
Durgā and Gadādhara for *ka*, Cakrin and Jayā for *kha*, and likewise Śaṅkhadhara for *ga*.
Vijaya is to be known as accompanied by Sahita; Śārṅgin is joined with Viraja. Hariklinna and Vasumatī are the two deities; Kṛṣṇa and Vasundharā [are likewise]. 22.
Govinda, Vasudeva, Śauri, Vasudhā, Madhusūdana, Sandhyāyuti, Dayāyukta, Vāmana, and likewise Śrīdhara. (23)
Trivikrama is accompanied by Harṣā and Medhā;
Khaḍgin is with Prabhā, Muṣalin with Caṇḍā, and Aṅkuśin [is accompanied by her]. 24.
Likewise, Pradyumna, endowed with devotion, is accompanied by Vilāsinī and possesses the form of a boar, together with Dharaṇī and Rati. ||25||
Satya was with Ūṣā, and after him was Aniruddha;
Yajñeśa was with Umā, and Śrī Rāma was endowed with compassion. ||26||
The Lord of the World, the descendant of Bhrigu, is to be known as accompanied by Ākṛṣṭi;
likewise, he in the form of the Tortoise is accompanied by Ugrā and joined with Dhṛti. (27)

Hayagrīva is endowed with speech; Janārdana is joined with the primordial [state]; Bala’s younger brother is [manifest] as a form; Bāla is [defined] by prosperity; and Gadāgraja is [defined] by purity.
Dāmodara, endowed with nourishment; the lotus-eyed one, endowed with contentment;
the sacrifice joined with oblations; and likewise, the wide-striding one.
Śraddhāyukta, Nṛsiṃha, and Saṃhṛtya, along with those beginning with Yā (Yāmya), Dhātu, Prāṇa, Jīvaka, and Krodha, are likewise the destroyers of the self.
When this is done, one becomes qualified for the practice of devotion;
therefore, this renunciation which accomplishes devotion should be performed with effort. (31)
Thus ends the second chapter in the Bhakticandrikā.
Chapter Three:
I shall now proclaim the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa), according to their respective locations and in due order.
By which the body certainly becomes composed of mantra at that very moment. ||1||
One should place [the syllables] in sequence upon the head, forehead, face, throat, heart, belly, navel, penis, the region of the knees, and the two feet. 2.
The practitioner, being well-composed and wise, should place the syllables of the mantra,
conjoined with the moon (the bindu), upon the fingers of both hands.
Then, with undistracted mind, one should perform the rites for the seer and so forth in their proper order.
For this mantra, Nārada is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi), and the meter (chandas) is said to be [the gāyatrī]. ||4||
The deity is Gāyatrī; Kṛṣṇacaitanya is the embodiment of rasa. The seed-syllable (bīja) is known as kāma-premā, and Svāhā is proclaimed as the power (śakti). ||5||
The primordial Śakti, the presiding deity, is [to be worshipped] by those most skilled in mantra everywhere—in the head, face, heart region, the banner, and the feet. (6)
One should place [the mantra] upon the limbs of the person to be protected; such is the sequential application (viniyoga).
Then, having fashioned five mantra-limbs from the words, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the mantra.
The practitioner should fashion the limbs with the syllables of the mantra according to the sequential yoga;
he should fashion the limb with the desire-mantra, and "Namaḥ to the Heart" is supreme. (8)
With "premṇā ca śirase svāhā" and also "śikhāyai vaṣaṭ," [one worships];
with "kṛṣṇeti kavacāya huṃ" and thereafter "caitanyāya."

"Vauṣaṭ to the three eyes," "Svāhā to the weapon," and "Phaṭ"—thus the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) is prescribed using all the syllables of the mantra. In this very same manner, one should perform the ritual placement of the hands (karanyāsa) with a concentrated mind. ||10||
Then, according to the prescribed rite, one should worship the seat (pīṭha) within one's own body;
having conceived it in the heart, it should be contemplated as being situated layer upon layer, beginning with the syllable Om.

He joined [the elements] to the foundational power (ādhāraśakti), to the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), to the tortoise (kūrma), to Ananta, to the earth, and then salutation to the ocean of milk. ||12||
One should go to Śvetadvīpa at that very place, to the jeweled pavilion;
there, one should worship Dharma and Jñāna on the right and left shoulders and on the two thighs. 13.
Then follow dispassion and sovereignty, each ending in the dative case;
furthermore, unrighteousness and ignorance are placed at the mouth, the banner, and on the two sides. (14)
One should worship Avairāgya and Anaiśvarya within the pavilion; in the cardinal directions and the center, one should worship the Kalpavṛkṣa tree, and below that, the jeweled altar.
Upon that [lotus] is the jewel-throne, and there also the very root of bliss (Ānandakanda),
the stalk of consciousness (Saṃvinnāla), and the lotus complete with its pericarp and filaments.
Then, the remainder [is placed] upon the pericarp: the mandalas of the Sun, Moon, and Fire, joined with the Praṇava and its limbs, and accompanied by their respective digits. ||17||
Likewise, [he meditates on] the Sattva, Rajas, Tamas, the Moon, the Tastes (rasa), and the Imperishable (akṣara);
then the Self (ātman) together with its power (śakti), both internal and supreme;
and then the "Knowledge-Self" (jñānātman). From that, he [places] the sixteen powers of the seat (pīṭha) as one.
Lakṣmī, Vasumatī, Bhadrā, Vimalā, Kamalāmalā, Arundhatī, Gāndhārī, Kṣamā, Śānti, and Haripriyā. ||19||
Rati, Kānti, Dhṛti, Satyā, Subhadrā, and Viṣṇupriyā are to be known as the Śaktis of the central region; these indeed are the Pīṭha-Śaktis. ||20||
The Blessed Lord Vāsudeva is declared to be the heart of the Vedas;
therefore, one should say "Viṣṇuṃ" followed by "jñeyaṃ," and then "sarvabhūtātmane. (21)
"Salutation to the one whose nature is the lotus-seat of the yoga of the conjunction of all selves.
Having thus worshipped the seat and having again performed the binding of the directions (digbandhana), [one should proceed]. ||22||
Placing his hands palms-upward upon his own lap, he should meditate on Śrī Puruṣottama.
Having reached the bank of the celestial river at Navadvīpa, the abode of people, [he was honored] by Brāhmaṇas, Paṇḍitas, Bhaṭṭas, Ācāryas, and Cakravartins. ||24||
It was attended by poets and sovereign poets, by discerning connoisseurs of poetry,
by physicians learned in the medical sciences, and by astrologers.

By generous donors, men of knowledge, the fortunate, those learned in the Vedas, and Vaiṣṇavas, [he should be worshipped] with karavīra flowers—both white and red—and the four kinds of śatapatra lotuses. ||26||
Furthermore, at that place frequented by the base of a kadamba tree,
there is a divine and enchanting spot attended by fragrant breezes.
She was surrounded by excellent devotees endowed with various dispositions, who held pairs of garlands in their hands and cried out, "Victory to Gaurī! [28]
Gradually, surrounded by seven enclosures and adorned with divine garments and ornaments,
there stands in their midst a divine, square, comfortable seat.
Endowed with a state of devotion, one should contemplate Him seated there. ||30||
One should meditate upon Him, resplendent with the luster of molten gold, wearing white garments with red borders,
seated upon a divine crimson throne; His lotus-face is graced with a smile, His two eyes are red,
and His chest, anointed with sandalwood paste, is adorned with a pair of shimmering *mālatī* garlands.
Caitanya, adorned with divine ornaments, the crest-jewel of the twice-born, consecrated by garlands of devotees. ||31||
Having meditated thus, the excellent practitioner, having seated [the deity] upon the worshiped pedestal from the center of the heart-lotus, should ask questions such as "Welcome" and so forth. (32)
With the mind and the root mantra, one should offer the arghya at the head,
followed by the pādya, the ācamanīya, and then the madhuparka.
Thus ends the third chapter of the Bhakticandrikā.
Now begins the fourth chapter:
[On] initiation for one possessing devotion, for the purpose of attaining perfection in mantra.
I shall explain [this work], which brings pleasure to the Blessed One, for the sake of accomplishing the desired goals of disciples. ||1||
Without which there would be no accomplishment of mantra even through ten million recitations and the like;
having seen this in the Kalpa, one who desires to speak [the truth] should never recite a mantra [without it]. (2)

Just as there are various objects for sacrificial fees within this realm of the universe, so too is the rite of offering one's own body the prescribed method for the sacrificial fee in that [highest] state. (3)
Next, first of all, the characteristics of the disciple and the teacher are stated. ||4||
A devotee who is daily proficient in explaining the reality of the methods of devotion, intent upon the narrative of Brahman, established in the singular reality of the Blessed Lord,
tranquil, self-controlled, devoted to no other means, and endowed with virtuous latent impressions— [such a one is fit for this].
With devotion, one should take refuge in the venerable Guru, following him constantly, free from deceit, and ever tranquil. ||5||
Approaching his guru, he who perceives his own karma bowed with devotion and spoke these words:
"I am one who has always been a partaker of unbearable suffering."
O Treasure of Compassion, show mercy to me! ||6||
O ocean of compassion, protect me— who am submerged in saṃsāra, prostrate before you, and behold nothing else— forever;
grant me the very method for serving that which I most desire.
He made the disciple, who had approached him, a follower of the beneficial teaching of the Kurus.
When the month, lunar mansion, lunar day, and weekday are auspicious, and at a favorable moment,
the self-controlled preceptor, being composed, personally commences the rite of initiation.
Surrounded by his disciple with garments, ornaments, flowers, and sandalwood paste, the wise one, adorned with these, diligently purified the ground. ||9||
Having placed there a seat made of cloth, deerskin, and kuśa grass in that order, the pure mantra-practitioner, with palms joined in reverence, should purify it with mantras. (10)

And here, having sat down in the svastika posture upon a seat consecrated with Merupṛṣṭha and other mantras, facing the eastern direction and bearing the vertical sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍraka), [one should proceed].
Having consecrated the perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should purify both hands;
then, having prostrated, one should place the lineage of gurus and Gaṇeśvara on the left side.
Having placed the Goddess to his right in front and Kṣetrapāla to his rear,
and having performed the ritual of the palm-claps (tāla) and the binding of the directions (digbandhana) according to the rules, he becomes free from obstacles.

Performing the purification of the body through the very sequence of elemental purification (bhūtaśuddhi), he established the individual soul (jīva) and other principles within the body according to the prescribed order of ritual placement (nyāsa). ||14||

Having worshipped the sacred seat (pīṭha) within one's own body, and having established the Great Lord there through meditation alone, one should worship Him with the root mantra (mūla-mantra) in due order by means of the mind. ||15||
Having become absorbed in that [deity], I shall perform the external worship;
I shall unwearyingly carry out the ritual placement of the *arghya* offering according to the proper sequence. (16)
The wise man should draw three excellent mandalas on the ground to the left, one above the other, each endowed with three, six, and four corners respectively.
Having washed the tripod with the Astra-mantra and placed it within that mandala,
one should worship it with devotion using perfumes and other offerings while remaining well-composed,
[visualizing] it as having the form of the fire-mandala by means of the fire-mandala mantra. (18)
Then, having washed the conch with the Astra-mantra, one should place it there;
one should worship that [conch], which is the form of the Sun, with the mantra of the solar disc (sūryamaṇḍala). ||19||
The wise one should place perfume, flowers, barley, and dūrvā grass into the conch with the heart-mantra; then, while the water is on the right, he should recite the mātṛkās in reverse order.
Without perceiving the true nature of that radiance, one should recite [the mantra] while imagining the nectar flowing from the moon;
with the thought that it is joined with that [nectar], one should fill the lotus of the head with water.
Having worshipped that portion with the perception of it as Soma and by means of the mantra of the lunar orb, one should establish the sacred fords (tīrthas) there from the solar orb; then,
having brought the Great Lord from the heart-lotus by means of His mantra, [one should place Him there].
Having displayed the gālinī mudrā, one should gaze at the water oneself with the mantra of the eye from the topknot (śikhā), and then veil it with the armor (varman) mantra. ||23||
Then, with the Guṇṭhana-mudrās, one should again place [the mantras] starting from its southeast corner:
the Heart at the end of the Armor, and the Eye in front.
One should worship that water in sequence with the mantras of the limbs and the weapons in the various directions;
then, one should perform the rite of immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) by means of the cow-mudrā and the conch-mudrā.
Having displayed and then carefully covered that water with the *matsyamudrā*,
one should recite the root mantra eight times and contemplate oneness.
Thereafter, with a serene mind, he should cast a drop of water from the conch into the water on his right for the sake of the deities of the water-lotuses. ||27||

With the remainder of that [liquid], the practitioner of mantra should sprinkle the ritual substances, himself, and [the vessel] three times; then, [he should place] the jar in the center of the mandala.

Upon rice and kuśa grass, accompanied by the worship of the Guru, Vighneśvara, and the sacred seat (pīṭha), one should wrap it with a pair of silken cloths and duly perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) together with the Tāra-mantra. ||29||
Then follow the five jewels, the five products of the cow, and the five nectars;
likewise, bundles of kuśa grass, white flowers, unbroken grains, and sprouts.
One should pour water scented with camphor, which consists of the *mātṛkās* and is most excellent, into each jar individually while reciting the root mantra. (31)

Having taken the pure essence of nectar, which has been consecrated three times with one's own mantra, or else having brought the decoction of milky trees and the like into the interior of a conch shell; 32.
Having filled it with that root-mantra, one should mutter the three-footed mantra there.
Having invoked all the holy fords such as the Gaṅgā, the oceans, and all the deities, and having cast the eightfold perfumes and the kalās, one should establish them there.
Having worshipped according to the rules, one should pour all the water into the jar;
then, having covered it, one should worship that jar which embodies everything according to the prescribed rite.

Having placed the beautifully written [mantra], situated in a vessel of yantra, gold, or other materials, into a jar, one should worship the support (ādhāra) and the other [deities] right there. ||35||
The lotus is endowed with eight petals, possessed of filaments,
complete with a pericarp, and is excellent, adorned with four gates and archways.
One should draw [the design] upon a vessel smeared with sandalwood paste using a golden stylus, provided with three lines and endowed with eight vajras.
One should draw a square seat in the center upon the pericarp;
there, one should write the seed-syllable of love (prema), and outside of that, an excellent hexagon.
Having drawn this yantra, which consists of the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja) within a hexagon and the syllable Bhuvas again within a quadrangle, and which is named Caitanyānanda; ||39||
He who, with a concentrated mind, holds [the image] in a golden vessel with saffron, attains devotion to the Lord characterized by love. 40.

There, one by one in succession, having worshipped the powers of the support (ādhāraśakti) and above them, and having meditated upon the Blessed One as he resides in the heart as before, [one should proceed].
Having unified the three unsurpassed splendors within the lotuses of the navel, heart, and forehead—resembling streaks of lightning—one should then [project them] outward with love. (42)
Having drawn [the deity] out and established it slightly upon the seat of worship with devotion,
one should then conceive of the form by means of the root mantra and subsequently invoke [the deity] once again.
Likewise, having established [the deity] with the eight mantras and mudrās beginning with āvāhanī,
one should offer the prepared arghya with the root mantra.
Then, having worshipped the God according to the rules with water for the feet and other offerings,
the wise one should again perform worship there with six handfuls of water at the feet, the heart, and the head.
One should worship [the deity] on the chest, the left side, and all the limbs with Tulasī and other offerings,
using white and red Karavīra and lotuses combined with sandalwood paste.

Having thus worshipped according to the rules, a person should then worship the limbs and the surrounding enclosures (āvaraṇas) in sequence with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, according to the prescribed ritual.
Therein, having requested permission from the Lord, he should cast [the offerings] from the base of his three-fold joined palms (tryañjali).
Having worshipped with flowers and perfumes the deities of the limbs, beginning with the heart-mantra, upon the square seat in the four corners starting from the southeast (āgneya), [verse 48].
The eye is in front, and in the four directions starting from the east are the weapon-deities,
possessing the luster of red, dark blue, pale red, white, and black fire.
Clad in golden garments and unguents, adorned with divine ornaments, they hold the boon-granting and fear-dispelling gestures; auspicious, they gaze with eyes moist with love. 50.
Outside of that, in the six corners, the Son of the Twice-born (Brahmā) is to be worshipped in front;
Gadādhara on the right side, and likewise Nyāsī Dāmodara.
To the left is the illustrious Nṛhari, and behind him is Gadādhara;
to the right is Datta, and to the left is Vāsudeva and Śivānanda. (52)

Those who gaze upon the lotus-face of the Lord with love, their bodies bristling with horripilation and holding divine garlands in their lotus-hands—these are to be worshipped according to the prescribed rite. 53.
Outside of that, at the tips of the filaments, are Nityānanda, Jagatpati,
the one named Ācāryādvaita, as well as Murāri and Śrīnivāsa.
Purī should be known as Mādhava, and also as Paramānanda;
likewise, he is Brahmānanda, Sannyāsī, and Nṛsiṃhānanda. (55)
Bhāratī and Keśava are to be known as experts in all branches of knowledge;
then there were Govindānanda, Govindadāsa, and Vakreśvara. (56)
Haridāsa, Mukunda, and Rāma, who was devoted to music—Haridāsa being the best of the twice-born—all wore garlands of sandalwood. (57)
Some are devoted to the names of Hari, while others are intent upon those very names;
they are endowed with the sprouts of love, their eyes radiant with tears of affection. (58)
Outside of that, in the middle of the petals, are Sārvabhauma, followed by Vallabha, Jagadānanda, Mukunda, and Raghunandana. (59)
Jagannātha, Śacīdevī, Govindaghoṣa, Kāśīśvara, Kṛṣṇadāsa, and Śrīdāmadāsa. ||60||
The one named Sundarānanda is a servant of the Supreme Lord;
he shall be Puruṣottamadāsa, and after him, Gaurīdāsa.
Then Kamalākara is to be worshipped; all [the deities] are to be meditated upon as having divine unguents, divine garments, and hearts overwhelmed by the essence of love. 62.
On the leaf, they should be worshipped outside of that; then, beyond that, Jñānānanda, Ghoṣaśrī, Vāsudeva, and Pratāparudra.
Rāmānanda, Rāghava, Pradyumna, Śrīsudarśana, Vāṇīnātha, Viṣṇudāsa, Dāmodara, and Purandara. (64)
Ācāryacandra, the Blessed One Candraśekhara, the one named Candaneśvara, and the scholar Śrīdhanañjaya; ||65||
All the devotees of the Lord should be meditated upon with minds overwhelmed by love for Gaurī, delighting in the name of Hari, and holding divine garlands in their lotus-like hands. 66.
Outside of that, in the various directions, the guardians of the quarters (dikpālas) should be worshipped with supreme devotion;
they are to be endowed with their respective seed-syllables (bījas) and adorned with their respective colors.
Indra, Agni, Yama, Nairṛta, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Kuvera, and Īśāna are in the directions, while Ananta is below and above. (68)
One should worship Lokeśa and his weapons in the directions outside of that;
and the eight forms beginning with Vajra in the lotus of the wheel, below and above.
Then, one should offer handfuls of flowers to him with the eight names, [visualizing] the forms of the Lord’s attendants, rich in their own characteristic marks upon their crowns. (70)
Having thus worshipped and having placed incense, a lamp, and an offering of food before him,
he should sprinkle them with the Astra-mantra and perform the rites of drying and so forth.
One should purify it again with the seed-syllables of air and so forth using the left hand;
having protected it with the *cakra-mudrās*, one should render it nectar-like with the *dhenu-mudrā*.
The adept, having performed the root mantra eight times and worshipped with Tulasī,
should offer [the oblation] with the root mantra, having consecrated the bell with that same mantra.
Playing [the bell] with the left hand, one should offer it repeatedly in a low tone;
one should display the incense seven times, from the feet up to the crown of the head. (74)
Taking the lamp and the food offering, one should offer it with devotion to the glorious Lord using that very mantra and the mudrā for presenting offerings. ||75||
O Hari, having placed this supreme offering, scented with camphor, back upon the ground, I present it to you; may you accept it with favor.
Having offered a mouthful with the mantra, one should display the *grāsamudrā*;
with the left hand, the form of an *utpala* lotus, and with the right, the five mudrās. (77)

Having fed [the deities] in due order and having offered the bali-oblation according to the rules, one should then present it to the planets and other deities. Then, having respectfully given a mouthful of water (gaṇḍūṣa) first,
one should perform the ritual three times, ending with the act of self-dedication (svārpaṇa), and thereafter perform the ritual placement (nyāsa).
Having established the deity in his heart with the *saṃhāra-mudrā*,
the diligent practitioner should then offer the remains of the offering (*nirmālya*) to Viṣvaksena and take a small portion for himself.

Having taken [it], becoming absorbed in that, and remembering everything as being of the nature of consciousness (cidātman), one should unite it with the jar, touch it, and recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. ||80||
Having brought the disciple, who has fasted on the preceding day, to one's left,
and having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and so forth, one should likewise bring a water-pot nearby.
One should consecrate the deity with water from a jar purified by recited mantras.
Then, having put on his garment and sipped water (ācamana), with a mind full of devotion and great serenity, the teacher, while seated in the presence [of the disciple],
meditated upon the Lord within his own heart.

Having worshipped himself and the disciple with water for the hands (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), and other offerings, and having clothed them in garments, he gazes upon the rudrākṣa with a divine vision. ||84||

Placing his hand upon the disciple's head, he should recite the mantra into his right ear three times according to the prescribed rule; and the disciple, contemplating oneness, should repeat it after him. (85)
Then, he should place [the mantra] into his hand, saying:
"May this mantra of ours yield equal fruit. (86)
The disciple, having received water together with *tulasī* while saying "May there be well-being," and having obtained auspicious blessings, becomes as he was previously envisioned in his mind. (87)

The preceptor and the disciple, with a tranquil mind and bowed in humility, should recite the mantra according to their capacity; from him, the disciple should learn the rules of conduct and other such matters. (88)
Then, having satisfied the guru according to the rules with devotion and wealth such as gold, the disciple should prostrate again and again upon the ground;
having offered his body, he should gratify the guru with respect. 89.
The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, the Guru is the Lord Maheśvara;
the Guru alone is the Supreme Brahman. Therefore, one should worship him first. 90.
One should always prostrate with the verse beginning "To him who is blinded by the darkness of ignorance," and so forth, to that Guru who imparts even a single syllable to a disciple. (91)
Whatever pleasing and delightful substance there may be, such as food, drink, and so forth, one should offer it to the guru first and then eat it oneself every day. (92)
The disciple, being peaceful and self-controlled, always devoted to service for the guru, observant of vows and ever truthful in speech, should diligently recite the mantra. ||93||
For these mantra practices, the wise one should recite [the mantra] one million times;
the fire-oblation (homa) shall be one-tenth of that, and the libation (tarpaṇa) one-tenth of that.

The consecration (abhiṣeka) consists of one-tenth of that; then one should feed Brahmins according to the rule of the tenth part, following the sequence of the procedures for the preliminary rite (puraścaryā). 95.
Thus ends the fourth chapter of the Bhakticandrikā.
Now begins the fifth chapter:
I shall now proclaim the hymn consisting of the description of each limb of the Lord.
By reciting this alone at the three times of day, a person shall obtain loving devotion. ||1||
A certain person, his mind agitated by the remembrance of Śrī Kṛṣṇacaitanya, his limbs covered with horripilation, and his eyes trembling with tears; ||2||
Having somehow regained his composure and bowed with reverence to his guru, he began to praise that moon among the twice-born, the great lord, with devotion. (3)
I bow to the teacher of the world, who possesses the luster of molten gold, who is dark as the Kali age, whose body is beautiful and long, and who brings joy to the heart of the illustrious Śacī. 4.
His beautiful, curled locks were bound with a string of shimmering pearls,
and his crest was adorned with a cluster of flowers rich in fragrance and consecrated with unbroken grains of rice.
His forehead was marked with a musk tilaka shining like a crescent moon,
and his playful, curved creeper-like eyebrows surpassed the bow of the God of Love.
His eyes are like sweet red lotuses with a flow of affection; his fresh, long nose is as glossy as a sesame flower. ||7||
Adorned with jeweled earrings shimmering on his glorious cheeks,
he has a beautiful, quivering peacock feather elegantly placed upon his right ear.
With a sweet smile and very tender, slightly reddened sprout-like lips, it is radiant with shining pearls set in smooth, slightly protruding rows. (9)
He has captivated the people of the world with his affectionate and sweet speech;
his chin is triangular, and his face possesses the luster of ten million autumn moons. (10)
With a neck like that of a lion, his shoulders were as exuberant as those of a great elephant in rut;
his beautiful, conch-like throat was adorned with three reddish lines. (11)
His chest was radiant with necklaces fashioned from pearls and coral, and his two arms hung down to his knees, shining with bracelets and armlets. ||12||
His glorious palms were radiant, marked with the auspicious wheel-signs;
his beautiful sprout-like fingers were adorned with the splendor of golden rings. 13.
Exceedingly smooth like sandalwood and agallochum, adorned with a series of horripilations, with a beautiful navel and a shimmering waist, and a belly slender as that of a lion. 14.
Her waist was bound by a girdle shimmering amidst garments of variegated patterns; her sprout-like feet were adorned with beautiful anklets that tinkled as they moved. 15.
His toes are adorned with nails that resemble the autumnal moon, and his lotus feet shine with anklets set with hooks, banners, vajras, and other jewels. 16.
Resembling ten million suns, with a splendor as lovely as ten million moons, possessing the beauty of ten million Cupids, and enchanting with ten million playful graces. ||17||
Manifestly the body of divine play, the body of sport, the embodiment of amorous passion;
in some places the form of the essence of aesthetic emotion, the manifest embodiment of radiant love.
He whose nature is name, whose body is name, and whose form is supreme bliss;
whose nature is devotion, whose body is devotion, and who sports in the conduct of devotion. ||19||
Possessing the entirety of playful loveliness, skilled in the sport of the tāṇḍava dance,
he is the treasure of nectar born from the jewel-ocean of Śacī’s womb.
The wondrous source of auspiciousness and joy for the entire world, his eyes languid with the intoxication of the ecstatic immersion in the rasa of the radiant rāsa dance. 21.
In some places, he was surrounded by devotees with divine garlands, perfumes,
and ointments, as they sang songs of aesthetic flavor, longing for that very rasa.
In one place, he was playing on the banks of the Gaṅgā, immersed in the joy of childhood;
in another, he was singing and dancing to the sounds of his own clapping hands.
Speaking with an exceedingly loud voice and displaying the prowess of a lion,
he at times shook the entire surface of the earth with his slapping of arms and the sound of "huṃ."
The three worlds were illuminated by the well-concealed state of being a cowherd girl;
all men and women attained their true nature without agitation. 25.

The eleven sense organs are rendered helpless by the relish of the aesthetic flavor (rasa) of their own innate nature; it is delightful with the playful arts of the sentiments of clever and sophisticated women. 26.
His heart's desire was overcome by a fraction of the sentiment of love for Gadādhara, and his mind was overwhelmed by the tasting of the essence of love for Narahari. ||27||
He who reveals the state of the beloved summoned by all the Bhāgavatas;
whose two arms are graceful in bestowing love; who is affectionate toward his devotees. 28.
The pair of feet known as "Love" (prema), the temple of glorious devotional love, which has enchanted the three worlds with the splendor of the aesthetic flavor of its own internal emotion. 29.
By the number of recitations of his own name, he made the surface of the earth Vaiṣṇava;
he brought joy to the people of the nine islands and auspiciousness to the community of Brahmins.

The lotus feet, which are accessible through fear, affection, deep love, and devotion, and which yield the excellent fruit arising from the sequence of the good fortune of all living beings without exception; 31.

The crest-jewel upon the head of the King of Dancers, the preeminent ornament of the illustrious Nāgara lineage, the adorning ornament for the throbbing crowns of all connoisseurs of aesthetic flavor.
The bee at the honey of his affectionate lotus-face followed by connoisseurs;
the crest-jewel of the illustrious twice-born lineage; the ornament of Navadvīpa. (33)
The lotus feet of the One to be served by non-duality, who is intoxicated by the nectar of the rasa of loving devotion;
the most beloved of eternal bliss, who fulfills the heart's desire of all devotees. (34)
The Lord, who is to be propitiated by devotion, who is attainable through devotion, and whose very form is devotion;
who is praised again and again by the foremost of devotees such as Śrīnivāsa, and by Sārvabhauma and others who are experts in the Vedas, Śāstras, and Āgamas. (35)
He who, being self-restrained, should thus constantly meditate upon the Lord of the Gods, and should always praise Him with a spirit of devotion at the three junctions of the day; ||36||
One who seeks the Dharma obtains the Dharma, the supreme Śrī Bhāgavata;
one who seeks wealth obtains wealth, as well as delight in the practice of service to Kṛṣṇa. (37)
One who desires worldly pleasures attains those pleasures through the practice of love and devotion;
one who desires liberation, being free from longing, attains release from the latent impressions of saṃsāra.
A seeker of knowledge obtains knowledge that cuts through desire and the cycle of worldly existence;
a seeker of poetry obtains the power of poetic composition characterized by the description of Kṛṣṇa. (39)
One who is childless obtains a son devoted to Viṣṇu, honored by the world;
one seeking refuge obtains the peaceful Śrīmad Bhāgavatam as a guru.
A person attains true devotion, which is charming with love and passion, for the lotus feet of the illustrious Śrī Kṛṣṇa Caitanya. (41)
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Individual Limbs," and the sixth chapter in the Bhakticandrikā.
Now I shall proclaim the supreme mantras that grant the accomplishment of all desires and purposes, for the sake of perfecting loving devotion to the moon of Kṛṣṇa-consciousness. 1.
The two-syllable mantra is "Kṛṣṇa," while Caitanya is considered the three-syllable mantra; the excellent four-syllable mantra is likewise the three-syllable mantra joined with "ṅe. (2)
And that supreme mantra of five syllables should be known as beginning with "prema" (love);
it should be understood as being encapsulated by "prema," with "caitanya" (consciousness) as the fifth [syllable]. ||3||
If the first [syllable] is *kāma* (namah), it is called the "six-syllabled" mantra;
if the six-syllabled mantra ends with *manmatha* (svāhā), it is considered a seven-syllabled mantra. ||4||
The mantra for Viśvambhara begins with *pra* and so forth; the supreme mantra for Kāma begins with *anu*;
the mantra for Śacīnandana consists of two *ṅe* [cases] ending in *vahni-jāyā* (the wife of fire, i.e., *svāhā*). ||5||
The eight-syllabled mantra begins with "Premā"; the nine-syllabled one begins with "Manmatha. This king of mantras is proclaimed to consist of ten syllables.
Of these, Nārada is to be known as the sage (ṛṣi), Virāj as the meter (chandas), Kṛṣṇacaitanya as the deity (devatā), and the supreme seed-syllable (bīja) is that which is called love (prema). ||7||
Śakti is said to be the consort of Fire (Vahni), the presiding deity of the syllables beginning with 'Sa'.
The arrangement of the limbs (aṅga-kalpanā) should be performed by means of [the mantra] called "Love" (prema), which possesses the six long vowels.
One should first perform the morning rites and other duties as prescribed by the scriptures;
[one should then visualize] a lotus endowed with eight petals, complete with a pericarp and filaments. 9.
One should draw a hexagon in the center and then write the seed-syllable there;
the excellent practitioner should worship the Blessed One there with devotion. (10)
His hair is bound with beautiful strings of pearls; his moon-like face is beautifully smiling;
he is adorned with sandalwood paste, aguru, lovely variegated garments, garlands, and divine ornaments. 11.

I worship Caitanya, who possesses a golden luster, who is sweet with the delight of the rasa of dancing and ecstatic possession, who is radiant in the attire of Kandarpa, and who is served by his own people. 12.

Having meditated thus, the excellent practitioner should daily worship with external offerings; then, having worshipped the guardians of the directions and their weapons outside, he should recite the mantra.
The recitation is said to be one hundred thousand times, followed by fire oblations and other rites in due order. ||14||
I shall further declare another mantra that bestows the fruit of all accomplishments:
"Veda-ādi-hṛd-bhagavate kṛṣṇacaitanya. (15)
This king of mantras consists of thirteen syllables; its sage is Brahmā, its metre is Virāṭ, and its deity is the one who assumes the form of the nyāsa. ||16||
Consciousness is the supreme bliss; the syllable Om (praṇava) is the most excellent seed-syllable.
"Salutation" (namaḥ) is the power (śakti); the application (viniyoga) is likewise for the sake of attaining devotion. ||17||
To the heart, salutation to Ācakrā, the beloved of Agni;
to the head, [salutation] to Vicakrā, the wife of Anala, the mistress of fire.
To Sucakrā, to Agnivaradā, and likewise to Śikhā—these are the six;
then to Trailokyarakṣaṇopetacakrā and to Agnipriyā. (19)

Likewise, the armor for the kavaca-mantra, preceded by the word asurāntaka; then the discus (cakra) ending in the dative case, and similarly the weapon (astra) with "svāhā" for the astra-mantra. ||20||
One should perform three sounds with the *nārāca-mudrā*.
Thus, the well-restrained practitioner should perform the ritual placement (*karanyāsa*) on the limbs and so forth.
Having performed the other [rites] as before, he should meditate upon [the deity] in the lotus of the heart. (21)
His body is beautiful with the luster of gold that has been thoroughly refined; his limbs, eyes, and arms are long;
his chest is smeared with sandalwood paste and adorned with a pair of fine *mālatī* garlands;
his form is graced by a pair of garments of slightly reddish hue; and he is rich in the arts of the graceful dance.
I bow to Caitanyacandra, who destroys all impurities and is accessible solely through loving devotion. 22.
In this manner, one should worship the Lord Janārdana with devotion in the various elements (dhātus),
together with his limbs, the lords of the directions, and the wielders of the thunderbolt and other weapons, in their proper order.
Thus propitiated by the best of practitioners, the Lord of the gods,
the Sovereign, instantly bestows devotion accompanied by detachment.
Now, I shall describe in due order the procedure for the worship of the mind named Prema (Love).
Brahmā is the seer, Anuṣṭubh is the meter, and the deity is the embodiment of Love. ||25||
Viśvambhara is the seed-mantra, and the one called Premā is [the deity] itself;
Śakti is declared to be Vahnivadhū, and the application is for one's own ritual action. 26.
One should perform the assignment of the limbs with a love that partakes in the six long vowels;
having performed the ritual placement of the hands according to rule, one should meditate with a concentrated mind.
One should meditate upon that child, serene and shining with the luster of the rays of the rising sun, seated on his mother’s lap, his body visibly manifesting supreme bliss and slightly swaying;
one should meditate upon that Lord, the Sustainer of the Universe, who removes the impurities of the Kali age, together with divine Brahmin women.
Being gazed upon with love, his face was smiling and adorned with red lotus-like eyes. ||28||
Having meditated thus, one should worship with devotion, in due order, by means of water for the feet, the respectful offering, and so forth. ||29||

Thereafter, one should worship with devotion the Mothers, adorned with divine ornaments and wearing spotless garments, in the corners starting from the southeast (Agni) and so forth, and subsequently all around upon the filaments themselves;
for Devotion, the Mother of the three worlds, is the primordial Śrī, the Consort of Indra, whose nature is splendor.
One should worship Śānti, Śakti, and Dhātrī, who reside in the petals following that, with perfumes and flowers.
Nityānanda, likewise Advaita, Murāri, Śrīnivāsaka, Jagannātha, and he who is known as Sudarśana—these are to be understood [as such]. ||31||
Gadādhara was renowned, as was the famous Nṛhari;
they wore divine garlands and garments, their hair standing on end and their eyes overflowing with tears. (32)
At the edge of the leaf, the wives of the Brahmins should also be worshipped with great effort—Mādhavī, Vaiṣṇavī, the Goddess, Śubhadā, Sundarī, and Satī. (33)

Kālindī, Lalitā, and [Rādhā], adorned with divine garments and ornaments, are to be known as the excellent neighbor-women, fair and dark respectively; outside of that, the foremost devotees are to be worshipped according to the prescribed rite in the various directions. (34)
Vāsudeva, Mukunda, Rāma, and Śaṅkara; then Nīlāmbara, Rāmadāsa, and Kavicandra. (35)
Haridāsa as well as Candraśekharācārya were there too;
all of them wore divine garlands and garments and were intent upon music. ||36||

Having worshipped the guardians of the directions and Vajra and the others outside that [maṇḍala], and then outside that again within the previously mentioned yantra, the wise one should recite the mantra ten hundred thousand times.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Bhakticandrikā.
Now begins the seventh chapter: I shall now declare the excellent mantra consisting of thirty-two syllables.
It pacifies all sins and is a fire that consumes all evil latent impressions. ||1||
It bestows the fourfold aims of life, is gentle, grants devotion, and is preceded by love; it removes evil intellect and bestows a pure intellect characterized by goodness. ||2||
He is to be propitiated by all, served by all, the fulfiller of the desires of all;
he is endowed with all authority and is the sole kinsman of all the worlds. ||3||

It is endowed with the power of universal attraction, destroys evil diseases, is free from the requirements of initiation rituals, and is devoid of distinctions between proper and improper times. ||4||
Worshipped by mere speech, independent of external ritual procedures,
bestowing fruit upon all through the mere touch of the tongue,
unrestricted by place or time, and highly esteemed by all disputants. (5)
I shall declare its extraction; listen with a concentrated mind.
The pair *hare* and likewise the pair *kṛṣṇa* are then reversed. (6)
Afterwards, one should recite that same "Hare Rāma" mantra in reverse order;
it is called "Hari" because it removes all sins.
Because he is the cause of attracting all living beings through the yoga of devotion, the Lord, whose body is composed of pure sattva, is called Kṛṣṇa by the virtuous. (8)
Rāma, who delights the world and brings about the severance of saṃsāra, is therefore declared in all the scriptures to be the bestower of liberation. ||9||
Kṛṣṇa is fond of being addressed; therefore, this mantra was composed by him according to the sequence of words used for addressing, and therein love is enjoined. (10)
This [Self] is the very nature of all names and the very nature of the body;
if there is love for it in one place, then it will exist in both. ||11||
Devotion occurs in every four-age cycle (caturyuga), and liberation likewise occurs in every four-age cycle; therefore, there are four names each for Kṛṣṇa and Rāma. (12)
From the practice of devotion comes the destruction of sin, and from the means of liberation [comes liberation];
in both of these cases, there are four names of Hari according to their respective names. (13)
Hearing the words of address, the Lord arrived there; ready to grant whatever was requested by his devotees, he prepared to give that very thing. (14)
By virtue of hearing their names, they do not desire anything at all; Hari, possessing such qualities, dwells within their hearts. (15)
The name "Rāma" has been applied to the mantra for the purpose of bestowing liberation;
since there is a contradiction between these two [meanings], tell me, what should be done by the devotees? (16)
In the beginning, through devotion, there arises liberation that cuts asunder the cycle of worldly existence;
likewise, there is devotion to the Lord (Bhāgavatī Bhakti), which is characterized by the mark of love. 17.
And so it is said:
"Without the yoga of devotion, there can be no liberation from the ocean of worldly existence;
and without that [liberation], devotion that bestows love for the feet of the Lord never arises. (18)

One who is endowed with knowledge through the destruction of ignorance and the experiences of pleasure and pain, who is devoted to love and devotion—such a person should be known as liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
Through this mantra, he becomes intent upon both the goal to be accomplished and the means thereof. 19.

I shall now declare its means of accomplishment here, according to the sequence of the prescribed rules: Nityānanda is declared to be the sage (ṛṣi), and Anuṣṭubh is cited as the meter (chandas). ||20||
The supreme essential form is Śrī Caitanya alone who is the deity;
the seed-syllable is the name "Kṛṣṇa," and devotion is declared to be the power. 21.
The primordial Śakti is the presiding deity whose very form is love;
her application leads to the attainment of love at the feet of the Lord. (22)
One should perform the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) according to the division of the syllables of the mantra:
"Hare Kṛṣṇa Hare Kṛṣṇa, obeisance to the heart. (23)
"Kṛṣṇa Kṛṣṇa" is for the head, *svāhā*; likewise "Hare Hare" is for the tuft of hair (*śikhā*), *vaṣaṭ*; and thereafter "Kavacāya Hum" is for the armor (*kavaca*). ||24||
"Hare Rāma, Hare Rāma" is for the two eyes with "vauṣaṭ";
"Rāma, Rāma" is to be known as the weapon mantra followed by "phaṭ. (25)
Then, one should perform the *karanyāsa* (assignment of mantras to the hands) in this sequence: "Hare Hare. ||26||
Then the mantra-practitioner should draw the yantra: a sixteen-petalled lotus, provided with three lines and equipped with gates and archways.
One should write the letters of the mantra on the petals with a measurement of two syllables each;
one should draw a hexagon in the center, within the pericarp, according to the prescribed rule.
One should place the seed-syllable called *premā* in the center and the seed-syllable *kāma* in the corners;
having worshipped the *ādhāra* and other elements even within this yantra, one should install [the deity] right there after meditating according to the prescribed sequence. (29)
Possessing a luster as beautiful as gold, uniquely adorned by pure beings, and singularly skilled in bestowing the gift of proclaiming his own sweet name—
may the Moon of Śrī Navadvīpa protect the universe forever.
Surrounded by his own attendants, the lord of the twice-born was a kinsman to the distressed. ||30||
Having meditated thus, one should worship the imperishable Supreme Self with devotion.
One should worship the deities of the limbs in the directions of the corners and the intermediate points;
they should be worshipped with devotion at the tip of the hexagon.
Nityānanda, named Advaita, Murāri, Śrīnivāsaka, Kāśīśvara, and Mukunda—these [are the forms] from the middle of the hair-tuft (keśara). ||33||
Gadādhara, the best of the twice-born, as well as the beloved Narahari, Dāmodara, Vāsudeva, Śiva, Ānanda, and Gadādhara. (34)
Rāghavasiṃha, Rāmadāsa, Sundarānanda, Śārṅgin, Gaurīdāsa, and then the venerable Parameśvara himself. (35)
Puruṣottamadāsa also, as well as those who take refuge in Vṛndāvana—Govinda, Vāsudeva, and Kamalākara. (36)
Outside of that, in the middle of the petals, are the Vaiṣṇavas devoted to bhakti;
Gopīnātha and Maheśa, clothed in white garments, are eternal. (37)
Jagāyi and Mādhava, as well as Vāsudeva and Acyuta, are to be known;
they should be worshipped with effort in the cardinal directions, their bodies covered with horripilation and tears of love. (38)
"Victory to Gaurāṅga! O Gaurāṅga, victory! O Lord Viśvambhara!"—thus they were constantly engaged in chanting, their speech faltering with love. (39)
On the tips of the petals, outside of that, are to be worshipped Yadunandana, Gaṅgādāsa, Keśava, and after him Kṛṣṇadāsa. (40)
One should worship Raghunātha and Viśvanātha, who are clad in blue garments and are eternal;
they hold divine garlands in their hands, are gentle, and are overwhelmed with tears of love and horripilation.
Then one should worship the other enclosures as before. 41.
The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is said to be accomplished by merely reciting [the mantra] ten million times,
according to the rule of performing four times the number of oblations prescribed for the ten-fold portion.
One should perform the recitation with diligence; no specific number of repetitions is prescribed.
The best of practitioners should recite using a rosary or by counting on the lines of the hand. 43.
The procedure for the recitation of mantras is declared to consist of a day of sixty *daṇḍas*.
There is no requirement here for bathing and such; one may perform it according to one's capacity.
He who accomplishes the mantra in this manner is indeed the best of practitioners. (44)
Thus ends the seventh chapter of the Bhakticandrikā.
The eighth chapter:
I shall now describe the practice of mantras, specifically for those who possess desires.
By means of which the accomplishment of all activities is achieved effortlessly. ||1||
With the mantra beginning with Vāgbhava, using a white lotus every day—
especially at the end of the night— one should worship the deity whose nature is Vāgbhava.
Having worshipped with white sandalwood paste, as well as incense, lamps, and other offerings, for one month while reciting the mantras a thousand times,
the wise person attains all branches of knowledge and stainless poetic genius.
Worshipping the fair-complexioned Lord Śrī with the very mantra from the *Śrīpūrva*, he [should worship] with flowers and with an ointment of white sandalwood paste. (4)
By offering one hundred and one white flowers produced from the *karavīra* plant every morning for one month,
while diligently reciting ten thousand repetitions of that mantra, what practitioner would not obtain prosperity? (5)
Having propitiated Gauracandra—who is endowed with all powers—by means of the mantra preceded by the Śakti-bīja, one who desires a son and has conquered his senses [shall attain his wish]. (6)
Having composed himself, he should offer twenty thousand oblations into the well-prepared *yonikuṇḍa* fire with red lotuses combined with white clarified butter.
Reciting the mantra one thousand times while remaining pure, he shall indeed obtain a pure Vaiṣṇava son within the course of a year. (8)

For those afflicted by fever and the like, or seized by the perils of disease, one should touch their head and recite the mantra consisting of the syllables beginning with "Nṛsiṃha" one thousand times; then that person shall surely be liberated from diseases. (9)

Desiring to know the reality of the self, one who is composed and devoted should, with that very [mantra] beginning with the *praṇava*, perform with devotion the festive installation of Gauracandra. (10)
Having propitiated [the deity] with Tulasī, Mālatī, and Jāti flowers sprinkled with sandalwood paste,
the practitioner, having conquered his senses, should perform one hundred thousand recitations of the mantra.
He attains supreme peace that brings about the cessation of saṃsāra;
distinguished and excellent knowledge arises—of this there is no doubt. ||12||
The entire world would become submissive, all men would become kinsmen, and the perfection of love, endowed with both knowledge and realization, would be held in the palm of one's hand. ||13||
For each specific desired object, there is independence regarding recitation and worship;
the rule consists of proficiency in the conduct of one's own stage of life, celibacy, and so forth. (14)
Having thus accomplished the mantra, one should drink water over which it has been recited a hundred times every morning;
by maintaining a restricted diet for one month, one will then become a possessor of the power of retention (śrutidhara). ||15||
Now, the procedure for the perfected application (siddhaprayoga). Next, the perfected application, which is approved by the virtuous, is also written down;
through which, by mere recitation, the intended mantra indeed becomes perfected. (16)

The wise one, subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya), should recite the mantra after encasing it with the *praṇava*; then, upon reaching one hundred thousand repetitions, he shall become one whose mantra is perfected (*siddha*). ||17||

Having interspersed the syllables of the mantra with the *vāgbhava* [seed-syllable] and reciting the mantra while remaining pure through restraint of speech for one hundred thousand times, the practitioner then becomes one whose mantra is perfected. ||18||
The excellent practitioner, being pure in soul and subsisting on a diet of milk, should recite the mantra joined with the lotus of the power of speech one hundred thousand times at midnight;
then the mantra becomes perfected, bestowing the fruits of all desired objects. (19)
Now, the procedure for *puraścaraṇa*:
Next, I shall explain the procedure for *puraścaryā* for the sake of attaining the power of the mantra;
without which there can be no success in mantras, much less in ritual actions. (20)
Having gratified the illustrious Guru with wealth, divine pairs of garments, and charming ornaments, as well as with love, speech, and service; ||21||
Touching my feet with both hands and prostrating myself on the ground like a staff,
I shall perform the supreme preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for this most excellent mantra.
"Grant me your command, O Blessed One, for the sake of accomplishing all desired aims.
Thus propitiated with affection by the Guru, the most excellent practitioner—
In a temple, at the root of an Aśvattha tree, in a flower garden, on a riverbank, on a mountain peak, on the shore of the celestial river (Ganges), or in the sacred field of Śrī Puruṣottama. ||24||
In one of those places, being pure and with a concentrated mind, [one should prepare] an area of two krośas all around for the purpose of eating, moving about, and other activities. (25)

One should prepare the place for recitation using wood from milky trees, having excavated it in the various directions; therein one should fashion the tortoise diagram (kūrmacakra) consisting of nine compartments. ||26||
One should draw the eight divisions there, starting from the letter known as the field;
that shall be the mouth [of the diagram] there, upon which a cloth, a deerskin, and kuśa grass are placed in ascending order.
There, the practitioner, with one-pointed mind, should place a seat consecrated with his own mantras—either a svastika, a lotus, or a bound posture (baddhāsana). (28)

Having sat down on the previous day, the wise one should mutter the Gāyatrī mantra according to the procedure for expiation, accompanied by the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) and sesame seeds and kuśa grass. (29)

Then, on the day of commencement, having bathed in the morning and sat upon his seat, he, being pure and having performed the formal resolve (saṅkalpa), should settle his body in the ritual placement (nyāsa).

With one-pointed mind, reciting the mantra neither too quickly nor too slowly, while meditating on the syllables of the mantra as the deity, he should perform it again ten times with the [ten] purificatory rites (saṃskāra). ||31||
One should recite with a concentrated mind from sunrise until midday;
for as many times as the recitation is performed on that day, so many times it should be done every day.
One should perform worship at the three times of day and offer material gifts to Hari;
one should eat only the remnants [of the offering], be moderate in food, moderate in speech, and pleasant in conversation.
One should avoid conversation with women as well as with Śūdras;
nor should one allow the mind to be enticed by various worldly desires. (34)

Having thus completed the full recitation of the mantra, one who knows the ritual procedure, being unable to perform the fire-oblation (homa), should recite the mantra four times the number required for the oblations—namely, ten parts (daśāṃśa). ||35||
The practitioner of mantras should perform the libation and the consecration according to the sequence of the ritual;
he should feed the Brahmins with devotion, and having accomplished his task, he shall become happy. (36)
Thus, taking the standard measure as a basis, the number [of recitations] is multiplied by four in the Kali age;
by such fourfold recitation, the mantra becomes perfected for men. (37)
Now follows the conclusion: Without dispassion, the accomplishment of mantra does not arise for men;
therefore, everyone, being dispassionate, should recite the mantra with diligent effort. (38)

Detachment, the purification of latent impressions (vāsanā), and emptiness regarding the body—both in this world and the next—arise from freedom from desire, as well as from delusion regarding higher realms, pride, hypocrisy, and the conjunction with egoism. ||39||
From stinginess and greed arises a habit-energy that is difficult to restrain;
for those whose minds are attached to it, the accomplishment of their purpose does not occur. (40)
The God will grant a boon when he is pleased; and how may he be pleased?
By abandoning evil tendencies and always being endowed with virtuous tendencies. (41)
With body, mind, and speech, the excellent practitioner, whose mind is intent upon his own dharma, should recite the mantra according to the prescribed sequence. (42)
When one worships Kṛṣṇa with devotion during the three daily junctures, being happy, constantly intent on His name, and finding joy in meditating upon His feet; 43.
Rejoicing at hearing stories of Him and intensely beholding His form—
in this way, whether indifferent or possessed of longing, one becomes concentrated.
Constantly intent on contemplating the command of his guru, ever regarding his guru as God himself,
Kṛṣṇa, with a joyful mind, then respectfully [bestowed this] upon the one who was free from worldly expectations.
It bestows upon one who has devotion for its own lotus-feet a love characterized by pure affection;
to such a person, it grants the supreme boon according to their desire. Otherwise, perfection is not attained even through millions of recitations and other such practices. (46)
By what means does dispassion arise, or from where does it destroy latent impressions, so that one thereby attains perfection which accomplishes all that is auspicious? (47)
The virtuous are indeed steadfast in the Vaiṣṇava scriptures and in the words of the guru;
through association with the virtuous and by the teachings of the scriptures, devotion to the guru becomes firmly established. (48)
In the established doctrine of the scriptures dedicated to that [reality], realization arises for people;
indeed, by means of those words, true knowledge is born according to reality. (49)
One discerns what is auspicious and inauspicious, specifically that which is to be abandoned and that which is to be accepted;
one who is practiced in renunciation should abandon [the former] and be intent upon grasping [the latter]. (50)
In this way, knowledge arises together with discernment;
by that knowledge, deep-seated latent tendencies are thoroughly severed. (51)

Just as one worships Kṛṣṇa with the intellect—blazing like refined gold—one should recite the mantra the prescribed number of times, for he is the singular embodiment of the mantra and the deity. (52)
Thus, the practitioner who has accomplished the mantra, having fulfilled his task, may dwell at ease according to his pleasure, with supreme joy, as one whose very body is supreme bliss. (53)
Thus ends the eighth chapter of the Bhakticandrikā.
